questions.question: What are the @Transactional propagation types and when would you use each?
questions.title: @Transactional — Propagation Types
questions.direct_answer: @Transactional propagation controls how a method behaves when a transaction already exists. REQUIRED (the default) joins an existing transaction or creates one. REQUIRES_NEW always suspends any existing transaction and creates an independent one. MANDATORY, NEVER, NOT_SUPPORTED, SUPPORTS, and NESTED cover more specialized scenarios.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to reason about transaction boundaries and choose the right propagation for audit logs, batch jobs, or compensating transactions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using REQUIRED everywhere without understanding that an exception in a nested REQUIRED call will roll back the entire outer transaction.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain NESTED (uses a savepoint so the inner work can be rolled back independently while the outer transaction commits) and contrast it with REQUIRES_NEW (fully separate transaction, separate connection).

sections.content:
Propagation defines how the transactional context is shared between caller and callee. Getting this wrong is a common source of data-consistency bugs — either over-sharing a transaction so an unrelated failure causes a global rollback, or creating too many independent transactions and losing atomicity.

`@Transactional` propagation types control what happens when a transactional method calls another transactional method. The seven propagation levels handle three key scenarios: whether to join an existing transaction, create a new one, or refuse to participate.

**REQUIRED** (default) — join the existing transaction if one exists; otherwise create a new one. This is correct for most service methods. If the inner method throws, the entire transaction rolls back because both methods share the same physical transaction.

**REQUIRES_NEW** — always create a new physical transaction, suspending the outer one. The inner transaction commits or rolls back independently. Use it for operations that must succeed regardless of the outer transaction's outcome — audit logging, notification sending, or idempotency token recording.

**NESTED** — create a savepoint within the existing transaction. If the inner method fails, only the work since the savepoint is rolled back; the outer transaction can catch the exception and continue. This requires JDBC savepoint support and is not supported by all JPA providers.

**SUPPORTS** — run in the existing transaction if one exists; otherwise run non-transactionally. Useful for read methods that benefit from transaction consistency when called from a transactional context but work fine without one.

**MANDATORY** — requires an existing transaction; throws `IllegalTransactionStateException` if none exists. Use it to enforce that a method is never called standalone — it must always be part of a larger unit of work.

**NOT_SUPPORTED** — suspend any existing transaction and run non-transactionally. Useful for operations like cache warmup or external API calls that should not participate in the caller's transaction.

**NEVER** — throw an exception if a transaction exists. The inverse of MANDATORY — enforces that the method is never called within a transaction context.
sections.title: Why REQUIRED Is the Default — and Why It Causes the Most Subtle Bugs
All Seven Propagation Types — Decision at a Glance
sections.content:
The seven propagation types answer one question: **what should happen to the transaction context when this method is called?** The answer depends on whether the operation should share the caller's unit-of-work, needs isolation from it, or must enforce a specific transactional context.

| Propagation | Existing Tx? | Behavior | Classic Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REQUIRED` (default) | Yes | Join it | Service layer methods |
| `REQUIRED` | No | Create new | Service layer methods |
| `REQUIRES_NEW` | Yes | Suspend + create new | Audit logging, notifications |
| `REQUIRES_NEW` | No | Create new | Audit logging, notifications |
| `NESTED` | Yes | Savepoint + continue | Optional sub-operations in batch |
| `NESTED` | No | Create new | Optional sub-operations |
| `SUPPORTS` | Yes | Join it | Read-only reporting queries |
| `SUPPORTS` | No | Run non-transactionally | Read-only reporting queries |
| `NOT_SUPPORTED` | Yes | Suspend + run non-tx | Legacy code, long-running reports |
| `MANDATORY` | Yes | Join it | Internal methods always called within tx |
| `MANDATORY` | No | Throw exception | Internal methods always called within tx |
| `NEVER` | Yes | Throw exception | Batch exports that must not hold locks |
| `NEVER` | No | Run non-transactionally | Batch exports |

The most important distinction in practice: **REQUIRED rolls back together.** If an inner `REQUIRED` method throws, the entire outer transaction rolls back. Developers who add an audit log call inside a business transaction and use `REQUIRED` find their audit log disappears whenever the business transaction fails — because the exception propagates and the entire unit of work (including the audit insert) rolls back. The fix is `REQUIRES_NEW`.

sections.title: REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED — The Two Isolation Mechanisms and When Each Fails
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`REQUIRED` rolls back together** — an exception in an inner `REQUIRED` call rolls back the entire outer transaction; an audit log inside a `REQUIRED` call disappears if the business transaction fails.
- **`REQUIRES_NEW` uses a separate physical connection** — suspends the outer transaction and borrows a new connection from the pool; the inner commit is permanent even if the outer transaction later rolls back; doubles connection usage under load.
- **`NESTED` uses a savepoint on the same connection** — inner failure rolls back to the savepoint; outer can catch and continue; outer failure rolls back everything including the nested work.
- **Self-invocation bypasses `@Transactional` entirely** — regardless of propagation type, calling a `@Transactional` method via `this` goes through the original object, not the proxy; no transaction management.
- **`REQUIRES_NEW` connection exhaustion at scale** — each `REQUIRES_NEW` call borrows a connection while the outer still holds one; in a high-throughput service with multiple audit calls per request, connection pool exhaustion becomes the failure mode.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Transactional` propagation controls what happens to the transaction context when one transactional method calls another. Getting it wrong produces data-consistency bugs — audit logs that vanish, operations that should be independent sharing a rollback boundary.

**`REQUIRED` (the default)**
- Joins the existing transaction if one is active; creates a new one if not
- Inner and outer method share the same physical transaction — an exception anywhere rolls back everything
- The audit log trap: write an audit log inside a `REQUIRED` call and the outer transaction fails — the audit log disappears with it

**`REQUIRES_NEW`**
- Always creates a new, independent transaction, suspending the outer one
- Uses a separate database connection — the inner commit is permanent even if the outer transaction later rolls back
- The right choice for audit logging and notifications that must persist regardless of the business outcome
- The cost: two open connections simultaneously; under high load with many `REQUIRES_NEW` calls per request, connection pool exhaustion becomes the failure mode

**`NESTED`**
- Creates a savepoint within the same physical connection
- Inner failure rolls back to the savepoint; the outer transaction can catch the exception and continue
- Outer failure rolls back everything — all work on the same connection
- Lower resource cost than `REQUIRES_NEW` but requires JDBC savepoint support

Regardless of propagation type: calling a `@Transactional` method via `this` bypasses the proxy — no transaction management at all. The propagation setting has no effect on self-invocation.

questions.question: How do Spring profiles work? Explain @Profile and spring.profiles.active.
questions.title: Spring Profiles (@Profile, spring.profiles.active)
questions.direct_answer: Spring profiles allow you to register beans conditionally based on the active environment. A bean annotated with @Profile("prod") is only created when the 'prod' profile is active. Profiles are activated via spring.profiles.active in application.properties, an environment variable, a JVM argument, or programmatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to configure environment-specific beans (datasources, mocks, feature flags) and understanding of profile inheritance.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hardcoding environment-specific values in beans instead of using profiles, or not knowing that multiple profiles can be active simultaneously.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain profile groups (spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring) introduced in Spring Boot 2.4, and the difference between default profile and fallback profile behavior.

sections.content:
Profiles provide a first-class mechanism for separating environment-specific configuration. Rather than using if/else logic or property placeholders throughout your beans, you declare entire bean graphs that are only wired in specific environments. Spring Boot extends this to application.properties files (application-prod.properties) and profile groups.

Spring Profiles provide a mechanism to conditionally register beans and load configuration based on the active environment — development, staging, production, test. They are one of the core building blocks for environment-specific behavior in Spring Boot applications.

**Defining profile-specific beans:** Annotate a `@Configuration` class or individual `@Bean` method with `@Profile("dev")`. The bean is only registered when the `dev` profile is active. You can use negation (`@Profile("!prod")`) to register a bean in all profiles except production.

**Activating profiles:** Set `spring.profiles.active=dev,local` in `application.properties`, as an environment variable (`SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`), a JVM argument (`-Dspring.profiles.active=dev`), or programmatically via `SpringApplication.setAdditionalProfiles()`. Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously.

**Profile-specific property files:** Spring Boot loads `application-{profile}.yml` (or `.properties`) for each active profile. Properties in profile-specific files override those in `application.yml`. This is the primary mechanism for environment-specific configuration: database URLs, logging levels, feature flags.

**Profile groups (Spring Boot 2.4+):** `spring.profiles.group.production=proddb,prodmq` defines a group so activating `production` automatically activates `proddb` and `prodmq`. This reduces the number of profiles you need to explicitly list.

**Testing:** `@ActiveProfiles("test")` on integration test classes activates the `test` profile, loading `application-test.yml` with in-memory databases, mock service URLs, and debug logging. This isolation ensures tests never accidentally hit production resources.
sections.title: Why Profiles Exist: Environment-Specific Configuration Without Code Changes
Define Profile-Specific Beans
sections.description: Annotate beans or @Configuration classes with @Profile. The bean is registered only when the named profile is active. You can negate a profile with '!' or use logical expressions.

sections.title: Activate Profiles
sections.description: Profiles can be activated through multiple mechanisms. Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously.
sections.content:
Spring profiles can be activated through multiple mechanisms, and they follow a **priority order** that matters when the same property is set in different places. The highest-priority source wins.

**Command-line arguments** have the highest priority. `--spring.profiles.active=prod` overrides everything else. This is the standard for containerized deployments where the orchestrator (Kubernetes, ECS) passes environment configuration at launch.

**Environment variables** are next: `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`. This is the Docker-friendly approach — you set it in the Dockerfile or the container spec.

**`application.properties`** is the lowest priority: `spring.profiles.active=dev`. This is typically the developer default — local development runs with `dev` unless overridden.

```properties
# application.properties — developer default
spring.profiles.active=dev

# Override via command line:
# java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

# Override via environment variable (Docker/K8s):
# SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
```

Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously — `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring` activates both. Beans annotated with either `@Profile("prod")` or `@Profile("monitoring")` will be registered.

sections.title: Profile-Specific Property Files
sections.description: Spring Boot loads application-{profile}.properties (or .yml) automatically when a profile is active. Profile-specific properties override the base application.properties.
sections.code:
# application.properties (base)
app.name=InterviewExplainer
logging.level.root=INFO

# application-prod.properties (loaded when prod is active)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://prod-db:5432/app
logging.level.root=WARN

# application-dev.properties (loaded when dev is active)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:devdb
logging.level.com.app=DEBUG
sections.content:
Beyond beans, profiles control which **property files** Spring loads. The naming convention is `application-{profile}.properties` (or `.yml`). When the `prod` profile is active, Spring loads both `application.properties` (base) and `application-prod.properties` (override). Profile-specific properties **take precedence** over base properties.

This is how you vary configuration like database URLs, logging levels, and feature flags without touching code. The base file defines defaults; the profile file overrides what's different.

```properties
# application.properties (base — always loaded)
app.cache.ttl=60s
logging.level.root=INFO

# application-dev.properties (loaded when 'dev' profile active)
logging.level.root=DEBUG
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

# application-prod.properties (loaded when 'prod' profile active)
app.cache.ttl=3600s
logging.level.root=WARN
```

A common mistake is putting production secrets directly in `application-prod.properties` and committing them to version control. Profile-specific files should contain non-sensitive overrides. Secrets belong in environment variables, Vault, or AWS Secrets Manager — injected at runtime, never stored in the repository.

sections.title: Profile Groups (Spring Boot 2.4+)
sections.description: Profile groups let you activate multiple fine-grained profiles with a single name. This avoids long comma-separated profile lists in deployment scripts.
sections.code:
# application.properties
# Activating 'production' activates prod + monitoring + security-hardened
spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security-hardened

# Activating 'local' activates dev + mockservices
spring.profiles.group.local=dev,mockservices

# Then in deployment:
spring.profiles.active=production
sections.content:
Spring Boot 2.4 introduced **profile groups**, which solve the problem of activating multiple related profiles together. Before groups, deploying to production meant setting `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring,security` — a list that grows with every new concern and is easy to get wrong.

With groups, you define composite profiles in `application.properties` and activate just the group name.

```properties
# Define groups — activating 'production' activates all three
spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security
spring.profiles.group.development=dev,local-cache,debug-logging

# Now just activate the group
spring.profiles.active=production
# Equivalent to: spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring,security
```

Groups keep environment configuration **manageable as the number of concerns grows**. Instead of every deployment script knowing which individual profiles to activate, it activates a single semantic group. Adding a new monitoring profile means editing the group definition in one place, not updating every deployment pipeline.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Profile("!prod")` registers in all profiles except production** — negation syntax enables beans that exist in every environment except one; common for debug tooling and test data seeders.
- **Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously** — `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring` activates both; beans annotated with either profile are registered.
- **Profile-specific property files override the base** — `application-prod.properties` overrides `application.properties` for any key present in both; the base file provides defaults.
- **Profile groups (Spring Boot 2.4+)** — `spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security` lets you activate a composite with a single name; keeps deployment scripts from growing long profile lists.
- **Activation priority: command-line > env var > `application.properties`** — `--spring.profiles.active=prod` on the command line overrides `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE` env var, which overrides the property file.
- **`@ActiveProfiles("test")` in tests** — activates the `test` profile for `@SpringBootTest`, loading `application-test.properties` with H2, mock service URLs, and debug logging.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring profiles let you register different bean graphs and load different property files based on the active environment — without changing code or rebuilding the artifact. The same JAR behaves differently in dev, staging, and production based on which profiles are active.

**Profile-specific beans**
- `@Profile("prod")` on a `@Bean` or `@Configuration` class — only registered when `prod` is active
- `@Profile("!prod")` — registered in every profile except production; common for debug tooling and mock services
- Multiple active profiles at once: `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring` — beans from both profiles are registered

**Activating profiles — priority order**
- Command-line `--spring.profiles.active=prod` — highest priority, overrides everything else
- Environment variable `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` — Docker and Kubernetes standard
- `spring.profiles.active=dev` in `application.properties` — developer default, lowest priority

**Profile-specific property files**
- `application-prod.properties` loads automatically when `prod` is active and overrides the base `application.properties` for any key present in both
- Base file sets defaults; profile files override what is environment-specific

**Profile groups (Spring Boot 2.4+)**
- `spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security` — activate `production` and all three sub-profiles activate automatically

In tests, `@ActiveProfiles("test")` loads `application-test.properties` — typically with an H2 in-memory database, mock service URLs, and verbose logging. Tests never accidentally hit production resources.
